hmmt-nov-2019-team-01.title: Compare with the total
hmmt-nov-2019-team-01.body:
Let Marc's drink contain $w$ ounces of water and $j$ of juice, with $w+j=12$, $w,j>0$. The total water drunk is $6w$ and the total juice is $8j$, so the total amount of liquid is $6w+8j$. Because $w,j>0$,
$$6(w+j)<6w+8j<8(w+j),\quad\text{i.e.}\quad 72<12\cdot(\text{number of people})<96.$$
(The total liquid is $12N$ for $N$ people.) So $6<N<8$ and $N=7$.

**Answer: 7**

hmmt-nov-2019-team-02.title: Upper bound and a cyclic construction
hmmt-nov-2019-team-02.body:
**Upper bound.** To receive an item a student needs at least $2$ votes for it: if the winner had only $1$ vote, every other student would have at most $0$ votes, but there are $2019$ votes to distribute. Each voter votes for a given student at most once, so a given student receives at most $2019$ votes in total. Hence he wins at most $\lfloor2019/2\rfloor=1009$ items.

**Construction.** Name the students by residues mod $2019$, and let the favoured student be $0$. Use $N=1009$ items. In item $i$ ($1\le i\le1009$), every voter $v$ votes for student $v+i$ (mod $2019$), except voter $i$, who votes for student $0$.

- In item $i$, student $0$ gets the vote of voter $-i$ (who votes for $-i+i=0$) and the vote of voter $i$: two votes (note $i\not\equiv-i$). Every other student $w$ gets at most the single vote of voter $w-i$. So student $0$ wins every item.
- Voter $v$ votes for $v+1,v+2,\dots$ in successive items, all different. The only exception is that voter $v$ (when $v\le1009$) votes for $0$ in item $v$. By the shift rule voter $v$ would vote for $0$ only in item $2019-v$, and this is an actual item only for $v\ge1010$. So every voter votes for $0$ at most once, and no voter repeats a target.

Thus one student can win $1009$ items.

**Answer: 1009**

hmmt-nov-2019-team-03.title: Separate even and odd powers
hmmt-nov-2019-team-03.body:
Write $P(x)=a_0+a_1x+a_2x^2+\cdots$. Then
$$\tfrac12\bigl(P(10)+P(-10)\bigr)=a_0+100a_2+10^4a_4+\cdots=302503,$$
$$\tfrac12\bigl(P(10)-P(-10)\bigr)=10a_1+1000a_3+\cdots=29130.$$
Since every coefficient is an integer in $[0,99]$, these are base-$100$ expansions, read off two digits at a time: $302503\to a_4=30,a_2=25,a_0=03$ and $29130/10=2913\to a_3=29,a_1=13$.

So $P(x)=30x^4+29x^3+25x^2+13x+3$ and $P(1)=30+29+25+13+3=100$.

**Answer: 100**

hmmt-nov-2019-team-04.title: Multiples of 3 are losing
hmmt-nov-2019-team-04.body:
Claim: the player to move loses exactly when $3\mid N$.

If $3\mid N$ (including $N=0$, where there is no move), then $N-2^n$ is never a multiple of $3$, since $2^n\equiv\pm1\pmod3$. So every move goes to a non-multiple of $3$.

If $3\nmid N$, the mover removes $1=2^0$ tokens if $N\equiv1\pmod3$, or $2=2^1$ tokens if $N\equiv2\pmod3$, reaching a multiple of $3$. By induction on $N$, the claim holds.

So the first player wins for $N$ not divisible by $3$. Among $1,\dots,2019$ there are $673$ multiples of $3$, so the answer is $2019-673=1346$.

**Answer: 1346**

hmmt-nov-2019-team-05.title: Classify the solutions
hmmt-nov-2019-team-05.body:
Every integer $x$ works (the right side is $\frac{x^2+x^2}{2x}=x$).

For non-integer $x$ with $n<x<n+1$ the denominator is $2n+1$, so $x=n+\frac{k}{2n+1}$ for an integer $k$ with $1\le k\le2n$. Such $x$ all work: indeed
$$x^2=n^2+\frac{2nk}{2n+1}+\frac{k^2}{(2n+1)^2}=n^2+k-\frac k{2n+1}+\frac{k^2}{(2n+1)^2},$$
and for $t=\frac k{2n+1}\in(0,1)$ we have $-\frac14\le t^2-t<0$, so $n^2+k-1<x^2<n^2+k$ and $\lceil x^2\rceil=n^2+k$. Then the right side is $\frac{n^2+k+n(n+1)}{2n+1}=\frac{n(2n+1)+k}{2n+1}=n+\frac k{2n+1}=x$.

So the solutions in $(n,n+1]$ are $n+\frac k{2n+1}$ for $k=1,\dots,2n+1$: an arithmetic progression of $2n+1$ terms with average $n+\frac{n+1}{2n+1}$, so its sum is $(2n+1)n+(n+1)=n^2+(n+1)^2$. Summing over $n=0,\dots,4$:
$$\sum_{n=0}^{4}\bigl(n^2+(n+1)^2\bigr)=0+2(1+4+9+16)+25=85.$$

**Answer: 85**

hmmt-nov-2019-team-06.title: Cyclic quadrilateral
hmmt-nov-2019-team-06.body:
Let $M$ be the foot of the altitude from $B$ to $CD$. Then $CM=\frac{7-1}2=3$, $DM=4$ and $BM=\sqrt{25-9}=4$. So $BMD$ is a right isosceles triangle, $\angle BDC=45^\circ$, and likewise $\angle ACD=45^\circ$. Hence $\angle DPC=90^\circ$.

Since $\angle DPC=\angle DQC=90^\circ$, the points $P,Q$ lie on the circle with diameter $DC$, so $PQDC$ is cyclic. Then $\angle RPD$, the angle between line $PQ$ and $PD$, equals $\angle DCQ$ (the exterior angle of the cyclic quadrilateral), which is $\angle DCB$. Therefore
$$\sin\angle RPD=\sin\angle DCB=\frac{BM}{BC}=\frac45.$$

hmmt-nov-2019-team-06.title: Simson line
hmmt-nov-2019-team-06.body:
Since $AB^2+CD^2=1+49=50=BC^2+DA^2$, the diagonals are perpendicular, so $P$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $D$ to $AC$. Also $Q$ is the foot from $D$ to $BC$. As $D$ lies on the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$, the line $PQR$ is the Simson line of $D$, so $R$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $D$ to $AB$. Then $RAPD$ is cyclic and $\angle RPD=\angle RAD$, whose sine is $\sin\angle DAB=\frac45$ (the height of the trapezoid is $4$ and $DA=5$).

**Answer: $\frac45$**

hmmt-nov-2019-team-07.title: The difference sequence is periodic
hmmt-nov-2019-team-07.body:
For $2\le i\le19$ we have $b_{i+1}-b_i=a_{i+2}-a_{i-1}$ (when both sides make sense), so $a_{i+2}=a_{i-1}+(b_{i+1}-b_i)$. Thus $b$ together with $(a_1,a_2)$ determines the rest of $a$ (note $a_3=b_2-b_1$).

Suppose $a\ne\hat a$ both produce $b$. Then $a_1+a_2=\hat a_1+\hat a_2=b_1$, so $(a_1,a_2)\neq(\hat a_1,\hat a_2)$ forces $b_1=1$ and $\{(a_1,a_2),(\hat a_1,\hat a_2)\}=\{(1,0),(0,1)\}$; say $a=(1,0,\dots)$ and $\hat a=(0,1,\dots)$.

Let $d_i=a_i-\hat a_i$. Then $d_1=1,d_2=-1$, $d_3=0$ and $d_{i+3}=d_i$ from the recurrence. So $d=(1,-1,0,1,-1,0,\dots)$: since $a_i,\hat a_i\in\{0,1\}$, we get $a_i=1,\hat a_i=0$ for $i\equiv1\pmod3$, $a_i=0,\hat a_i=1$ for $i\equiv2$, and $a_i=\hat a_i$ free for $i\equiv0\pmod3$. The last condition $b_{20}=a_{19}+a_{20}=\hat a_{19}+\hat a_{20}$ holds because $d_{19}+d_{20}=d_1+d_2=0$.

Conversely, every such pair $(a,\hat a)$ gives the same $b$. The free positions are $3,6,9,12,15,18$, six of them, and different choices of free bits give different $b$. So there are $2^6=64$ such sequences $b$ (each is produced by exactly two sequences $a$).

**Answer: 64**

hmmt-nov-2019-team-08.title: Reflect B over AD
hmmt-nov-2019-team-08.body:
Let $F$ be the reflection of $B$ over line $AD$. Since $AD$ bisects the external angle at $A$, $F$ lies on ray $\overrightarrow{CA}$ beyond $A$, with $AF=AB=10$ and $DF=DB$. Hence $CF=CA+AF=22$.

Because $F$ and $B$ are symmetric about $AD$, $\angle FDB=2\angle ADB=\angle BDE$. Ray $DB$ is the same as ray $DC$, so $DC$ bisects $\angle FDE$. Also $E$ lies on ray $AC$ beyond $C$ (as $CE=33>CA$), so $C$ is on segment $FE$. By the angle bisector theorem in triangle $FDE$,
$$\frac{DF}{DE}=\frac{CF}{CE}=\frac{22}{33}=\frac23.$$
Since $DF=DB$, $\frac{DB}{DE}=\frac23$.

**Answer: $\frac23$**

hmmt-nov-2019-team-09.title: Count points for each laser
hmmt-nov-2019-team-09.body:
A beam at angle $n^\circ$ to the tangent creates chords each subtending an arc of $2n^\circ$, so the illuminated points are the multiples of $2n^\circ$ around the circle. The beam returns to $P$ after $\frac{360}{\gcd(360,2n)}=\frac{180}{\gcd(180,n)}$ chords, and these are all distinct points: $m_n=\frac{180}{\gcd(180,n)}$ points. The points of the two lasers coincide where the two cyclic groups overlap, which happens in $\gcd(m_n,m_{n+1})$ points. So the number of illuminated points is
$$m_n+m_{n+1}-\gcd(m_n,m_{n+1}).$$

Since $\gcd(n,n+1)=1$, the numbers $\gcd(180,n)$ and $\gcd(180,n+1)$ are coprime divisors of $180=4\cdot9\cdot5$. To make $m_n+m_{n+1}$ small we want both gcds large; the best coprime pair of divisors of $180$ is $20$ and $9$, giving $9+20=29$, with $\gcd(9,20)=1$ common point (just $P$), for a total of $28$. (Other coprime pairs give larger sums, e.g. $36,5\to41$; $45,4\to49$.) This is attained at $n=80$: $\gcd(180,80)=20$, $\gcd(180,81)=9$.

(A direct check of all $n=1,\dots,89$ confirms that the minimum is $28$.)

**Answer: 28**

hmmt-nov-2019-team-10.title: Count regions with Euler-type formula
hmmt-nov-2019-team-10.body:
Draw the diagonals one at a time. Each new diagonal adds one region plus one region for every point where it meets earlier diagonals (a point through which $k$ diagonals pass adds $k-1$ in total over the diagonals through it). So
$$\#\text{pieces}=1+(\#\text{diagonals})+\sum_{\text{points }p}(k_p-1).$$

Diagonal $A_iA_{i+3}$ crosses exactly four others ($A_{i\pm1}A_{i\pm1+3}$ and $A_{i\pm2}A_{i\pm2+3}$), so there are $\frac{2019\cdot4}2=4038$ crossing pairs. A point where exactly two diagonals meet contributes $1$ (one pair); a point where three meet contributes $2$ (three pairs); the official solution shows four cannot meet. So $\sum(k_p-1)=4038-T$, where $T$ is the number of triple points, and
$$\#\text{pieces}=1+2019+4038-T=6058-T.$$

A triple point must come from three consecutive diagonals $A_{i-1}A_{i+2}$, $A_iA_{i+3}$, $A_{i+1}A_{i+4}$. Two consecutive triples $i$ and $i+1$ would share two diagonals that meet at two different points, which is impossible, so no two cyclically consecutive indices $i$ give triple points, and $T\le\lfloor2019/2\rfloor=1009$. Hence there are at least $6058-1009=5049$ pieces.

Equality is attainable: start from a regular $1010$-gon $B_1\dots B_{1010}$ and define $A_{2n}$, $A_{2n+1}$ through the external angle bisectors of the $B_n$ so that $A_{2n-1}A_{2n+2}$, $A_{2n}A_{2n+3}$, $A_{2n+1}A_{2n+4}$ all pass through $B_{n+1}$ (this is the construction in the official solution), giving $1009$ triple points.

**Answer: 5049**
